A1.justification: Despite the changed title, both PDFs describe KLENT and share the principal experiments. Their complete main texts, equations, figures, tables, and appendices are readable and support reliable comparison.

before.justification: v1 reports original board-game experiments, component ablations, computational analyses, and Count Up game simulations in Section 5 and the appendices.

after.justification: v2 retains these empirical results and adds Matching Pennies simulations, architecture experiments, and additional algorithm comparisons.

M1.justification: Section 4 and Algorithm 1 retain the analytical policy update, policy/action-value networks, lambda-return targets, joint loss, and self-play/fitting procedure. The new architecture and regularization variants are experimental alternatives; the proposed KLENT procedure is unchanged.

E1.justification: v2 adds Matching Pennies, a simultaneous normal-form game, in Section 5.1. The five principal board games, 19x19 Go, and Count Up game are retained; Count Up moves from v1 Appendix L to v2 Appendix D. Stochastic and continuous-action environments are discussed but not evaluated.

E2.justification: Appendices I–J add evaluated Forward-KL, Entropy Reward, Discrete SAC, V-MPO, Munchausen DQN, and GRPO comparators. Table 2 also includes AlphaZero in the test-time MCTS comparison, whereas v1's corresponding 9x9 Go scaling experiment compared KLENT with Gumbel AlphaZero. The original principal baselines remain.

E3.justification: The original board-game protocols remain intact. Targeted additions include a five-game comparison using checkpoints trained with 800 million simulator evaluations and 800 test-time rollouts, a Matching Pennies regularization grid, and architecture controls including separate networks with approximately twice the computational cost.

E4.justification: v2 substantially expands diagnostic evidence: Figure 3 tests convergence boundaries, Figure 8 tracks policy-update KL divergence, Appendix H tests head/backbone sharing and an EMA variant, and Appendix I tests alternative regularization choices. Existing component ablations, hyperparameter sensitivity, rollout studies, and Count Up analyses are retained.

E5.justification: The new MCTS comparison in Table 2 explicitly reports means and standard errors. The existing learning curves and search-scaling experiments retain three-seed means and standard deviations. No increase in repeated-run counts or new significance-testing procedure is documented.

E6.justification: Principal learning curves and older appendix tables are retained, but substantial results are added. Table 2 reports MCTS average win rates of 32.2%, 53.6%, and 77.2% for AlphaZero, Gumbel AlphaZero, and KLENT. At 800 million evaluations, Tables 6–7 report 61%, 14%, 2%, and 3% for Forward-KL, Entropy Reward, Munchausen DQN, and GRPO, versus KLENT's retained 89%. Architecture and convergence findings are also added.

T1.justification: Beyond v1's analytical-update derivation and empirical equilibrium discussion, v2 adds Section 5 and Appendix C: local linear convergence under alpha(alpha + 2 beta) > ||R||_2^2/4, supporting Jacobian lemmas and proofs, a general-sum extension, and a bounded-horizon convergence argument. These constitute a substantial new theoretical component.

C1.justification: v1 centers its contributions on an efficient board-game algorithm and empirical component validation. v2's abstract, introduction, and conclusion make stability and convergence characterization central contributions and explicitly locate novelty in theoretical and empirical understanding of existing regularization ingredients. The principal efficiency claim remains.

C2.justification: v2 adds explanations connecting efficiency to branching factors, architecture/computation tradeoffs, and alternative regularization results. It discusses multiplayer and infinite-horizon proof boundaries and possible stochastic/continuous-action extensions. The earlier spatial-complexity explanation for action-value learning and Retrace extension suggestion disappear; the asymptotic-performance caveat remains.

D1.justification: v2 describes the added shared-head and separate-network configurations and their computational implications. It removes v1's explicit n-step/lambda-return formulas and MLP-head description. Default hyperparameters, optimizer settings, parallelism, hardware information, and existing implementation/checkpoint references are otherwise retained.

R1.justification: v2 substantially repositions the work as extending regularized-policy and game-theoretic research, explicitly comparing its convergence condition with Sokota et al. It adds literature supporting Discrete SAC, V-MPO, Munchausen DQN, and GRPO comparisons, while trimming historical TD-learning and Q-learning discussion.

P1.justification: The title, abstract, introduction, and conclusion are substantially rewritten. Related work and the problem setting are reorganized, value-learning exposition is compressed, and the appendices are reordered into four thematic parts with a contents list. These changes reshape the narrative beyond simply inserting new results.

P2.justification: v2 adopts a two-column main-text layout, rearranges benchmark and ablation panels into horizontal rows, adds convergence and KL-divergence figures and comparison tables, and redraws Count Up results for the main text. The Go spatial illustration and ablation-configuration table disappear; existing branching-factor statistics are additionally displayed in Table 1.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens v1's mainly empirical justification through conditional normal-form convergence analysis, targeted architecture and regularization tests, and broader MCTS comparisons. These additions better explain the design and test competing explanations for its efficiency. The finite-horizon proof presumes value-estimate convergence, new baseline configurations remain sparsely documented, and some method detail is lost, but these limitations do not outweigh the substantial gains in scientific support.
